  "text": "By morning Tobias had worn a pale place in the church door with his sleeve. He had sat against it through the night. When the verger came, he got up and said he had lost his key.

The verger offered to fetch the spare. Tobias thanked him. Neither moved.

From the churchyard they could see Maren's house. The door was shut. There was nothing in the window but the lamp, unlit, and a little of the ceiling beyond it.

He went there at noon with bread. He had bought two loaves and could not remember asking for the second.

The posts stood straight along the path. He counted them without moving his lips. At the porch he stopped and tucked the bread beneath his coat while he knocked.

No one answered. From inside came the smell of cold ashes.

He tried the latch. It lifted readily, but the door would not open. He put his shoulder to it once, gently, as though someone on the other side might be asleep against the wood.

Then he set the loaf on the sill.

All winter he passed that way. The bread remained. Rain darkened the crust; frost whitened it. No bird took it.

In March he brought a cloth to wrap it in.

There were crumbs on the sill. The lamp had been moved back from the glass, just far enough to make room for a plate.

Tobias stood with the cloth open in his hands.

Then he folded it and went to buy another loaf."

  "text": "The baker asked whether he wanted it cut. Tobias said no, then waited while she found a clean sheet of paper.

At Maren's house he took away the plate and brushed it with his sleeve. There was a blue flower beneath the crumbs. He had eaten from those plates before, though he could not have said when.

He set the loaf down and left.

Two days later the paper lay folded beneath the plate. He put it in his pocket. At home he smoothed it on the table, finding nothing written on either side.

After that he brought bread on Thursdays. Sometimes it was gone by evening. Sometimes it stayed until he came again, and he exchanged it without knocking.

In May the grass along the path needed cutting. He borrowed the verger's shears and worked from the gate inward. At the porch he found a cup of water on the step.

He drank standing up. Then he finished the narrow strip beside the house.

There was still no sound within.

Before leaving, he washed the cup at the pump and returned it to the step, upside down so that nothing would fall into it.

The following Thursday the door stood open the width of his hand. He could see where its lower edge had scraped the floorboards.

He knocked on the frame.

After a while someone moved a chair.

Tobias unwrapped the bread. He waited with the paper gathered in one hand until a woman he had not seen since autumn opened the door a little wider."

  "text": "Maren looked at the loaf, then at the paper in his hand.

“You can leave that,” she said.

He laid both on the table. The chair she had moved stood beside the stove. There was another under the window, with a basket of mending on its seat.

She lifted the basket and put it on the floor.

Tobias sat with his cap between his knees. While she found the knife, he watched a fly travel along the window's lower edge. The glass had been washed where a hand could reach it.

The first slice fell thick. Maren cut the next one thinner and pushed the plate toward him.

He stayed until he had eaten it. Neither mentioned Thursday.

The next week he brought a small plane as well as the bread. He showed her where the door caught, and she stood back to let him work. Pale curls collected against his shoes. When the door swung freely, she opened and closed it twice.

“There's a drawer,” she said.

He came back on Saturday for that.

By June the loaf was no longer waiting on the porch. Sometimes Maren met him at the gate. Once she asked him to get it cut, because her wrist was troubling her.

He forgot and carried it back to the baker.

On his return, Maren had set two plates beneath the window. His held the blue flower. He moved it a little to make room for the bread, and she brushed the shavings from Saturday out of the other chair before sitting down."
